subject: Access onramp recommendation for Acme Analytics private deployment

Subject: Private deployment connectivity — quick clarifying Qs

Hi Sofia —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Our infra team (cc'd) is trying to choose the best "onramp" for Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) and wanted a short list of tradeoffs. High-level constraints:

- We must avoid transiting customer data over the public internet where possible (regulatory).
- Latency goal: 15–35ms p95 from our app fleet in us-west-2 to the inference endpoints.
- We'd like predictable egress billing and simple key-rotation (KMS).
- We may need to burst to hosted capacity occasionally.

Can you confirm whether PrivateLink satisfies the non-internet requirement end-to-end, and what the operational differences look like vs VPC Peering and a S2S IPsec VPN? An advantage/disadvantage one-pager would be great.

Thanks,
Liam
Liam O'Connor
Head of Platform Engineering
Acme Analytics

Subject: Re: Private deployment connectivity — quick clarifying Qs

Hi Liam —

Short answers up front: PrivateLink provides an endpoint that keeps traffic on the cloud provider backbone (no public internet path), VPC Peering is also internal-to-cloud but has different routing/ACL characteristics and scale limits, and a site-to-site VPN crosses the public internet unless you use a dedicated interconnect.

I'll attach a concise comparison and a recommended pilot plan. Quick notes:

- PrivateLink (our usual recommendation when customers want isolated, private ingress):
  * Traffic stays on provider backbone between customer VPC and our service endpoint; public internet is not used.
  * Easy to expose a small set of endpoints/services; works well with endpoint policies.
  * No transitive routing — customer cannot use PrivateLink to reach other services in Redwood VPCs automatically.
  * Good for security reviews because the contract surface is limited.

- VPC Peering:
  * Low latency and high throughput inside cloud provider, but peering relationships can scale poorly for many VPCs.
  * Requires careful route table management and may complicate CIDR planning.
  * Transitive peering is not supported (depends on provider).

- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec):
  * Common fallback for on-premises datacenters.
  * Traffic traverses public internet unless private circuit (e.g., Direct Connect) is used.
  * Easier for legacy networks but more operational overhead (tunnels, BGP sessions, failover).

Recommendation summary (high level):
- If you want minimal attack surface and simpler security review: PrivateLink + strict endpoint policies.
- If you require full L3 access between subnets for complex architectures: consider Peering or a dedicated interconnect + VPC Peering.
- Use S2S VPN with redundancy only for on-prem or where direct interconnects are not possible; we can support VPN as a burst path to hosted capacity.

I'm looping in Kimberly and Karthik to propose an operational pilot (2-week) and the one-pager you asked for.

Best,

Team —

Quick internal notes to shape the pilot and the redlines for Acme's security team:

1) Security posture and auditability- PrivateLink: simplest audit surface (endpoint) and plays nicely with customer KMS for payloads; recommend we provide a short artifact (flow diagram + network ACL checklist).

2) Performance and latency- Peering can give the lowest deterministic latency if the customer is fully in the same cloud region and CIDRs don't conflict. Measured p95 differences between peering and privatelink are often <5ms in us-west-2, but peering can have less overhead for path length.

3) Operational overhead and scale- PrivateLink scales better for multi-account customers because no peering mesh is required. For customers expecting dozens of VPCs we should avoid requiring peering per VPC.

4) Cost model and egress predictability- PrivateLink usually has per-endpoint-hour + per-GB charges; peering is typically free for traffic inside the same provider (but depends on cross-account/region). VPN egress costs and variable latency make billing less predictable.

5) Edge cases / hybrid- If Acme needs deterministic L3 adjacency (e.g., for proprietary service discovery), peering + centralized NAT or a transit gateway is the proper approach. If they want least friction for security review and ability to control policies per-service, PrivateLink wins.

Proposed short pilot:
- Week 0: exchange minimal network details (CIDRs, route table owner contact, desired endpoints).
- Week 1: stand up PrivateLink endpoint in a test account; run perf tests using their test harness.
- Week 2: test failover to S2S VPN (two tunnels) for burst flows and measure failover behavior and egress cost samples.

I added a diagram and checklist to Drive: https://drive.google.com/open?id=1a2b3c-acme-onramp-diagram — please review and LMK any CIDR conflicts.

-Kim

Hi Liam / Anita —

Thanks for the detailed constraints. Based on your latency target, regulatory requirement to avoid the public internet, and desire for predictable billing, our recommendation is:

Primary: PrivateLink endpoints for your critical inference routes- Why: keeps traffic on AWS backbone, tight endpoint policy controls, smaller audit surface for compliance.

Secondary (optional resilience/burst): Dedicated S2S VPN tunnels to a transit VPC or Direct Connect (customer choice)- Why: provides a burst/fallback path to our hosted capacity and on-prem reachability if you need L3-level adjacency for certain services. If you choose VPN only (no Direct Connect), note that traffic to hosted capacity would traverse the public internet and we strongly recommend IPsec with BGP for failover.

When PrivateLink is insufficient (rare): VPC Peering or Transit Gateway- Use-case: when your application absolutely requires L3 connectivity between subnets (service discovery, complex multicast/legacy flows). Peering demands CIDR planning and doesn't scale as well for many accounts. Transit Gateway can centralize but has additional cost and ops work.

Action items we propose (I can schedule these with your team):
- Exchange CIDR and route table contacts (security + network ops).
- Kick off a 2-week pilot: PrivateLink in us-west-2 + performance tests; then test failover to VPN tunnels.
- Deliverables: one-pager (attached), secure network diagram (Drive link), and a short runbook for key rotation and incident playbook.

If this sounds good I'll send a formal pilot SOW and a timeline.

Best regards,
